approachQuestion.prompt:
Return the identifier at its first repeat

Input: an array of integer identifiers in event order. Return the value whose second occurrence has the smallest index. If no value repeats, return null. Example 1: [12, 5, 8, 5, 12] → 5. Example 2: [4, 4, 4] → 4. Example 3: [2, 7, 9] → null.
constraints: Return an identifier or null; do not reorder or mutate the input.
Assume integer-key hash table lookups and insertions have expected amortized constant cost under an ordinary non-adversarial distribution; this is not a worst-case guarantee.

options.text: Scan in order using a set. If the current identifier is already present, return it; otherwise add it. Return null if the scan finishes.
options.feedback: The set contains exactly the identifiers from earlier positions, so the first membership hit is the repeat with the smallest second-occurrence index.

options.text: First count every identifier in a map. Then scan events in order with a seen set: if the current identifier has a full count above one and is already in the set, return it; otherwise add it to the set.
options.feedback: This returns the correct first repeated identifier, but the full frequency pass and map are unnecessary: the input-order seen-set scan can return as soon as the first repeat is determined.

options.text: For each position, compare its value with every earlier position and return the first match found.
options.feedback: This is correct but brute force; it repeats earlier-position comparisons instead of retaining prior membership.

options.text: Sort a copy and return the smallest identifier that appears more than once.
options.feedback: The task asks which duplicate is encountered first, not which duplicate has the smallest value. In [12, 5, 8, 5, 12], this would return 5 by value ordering only by coincidence; use [20, 3, 20, 3], where it returns 3 instead of 20.

feedback.reason: Preserve the original event order; the first repeated value is determined by when its second occurrence arrives.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Check prior membership in event order” shown after your first answer, choose its expected running time and auxiliary-space pair under this explicit model: For this question, assume integer-key hash operations take expected amortized O(1) time under a non-adversarial hash distribution. State expected time on that basis; do not interpret it as an unconditional worst-case guarantee. Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input arrays and the returned scalar/pair, but includes every map/set and temporary structure.
constraints: For this question, assume integer-key hash operations take expected amortized O(1) time under a non-adversarial hash distribution. State expected time on that basis; do not interpret it as an unconditional worst-case guarantee. Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input arrays and the returned scalar/pair, but includes every map/set and temporary structure.

options.text: Expected O(n) time; O(u) auxiliary space, where u is the number of distinct identifiers seen before stopping or reaching the end.
Expected O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space.
O(n log n) time; O(n) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Each event is tested once and inserted at most once; the set keeps prior membership state until the answer is found or the scan ends.

details.analyzedMethod: The set stores values already encountered in the input order. A membership hit ends the scan immediately.
details.time: Expected O(n), with at most n expected-constant-time membership checks and n expected-constant-time insertions under the stated hash model.
details.additionalSpace: O(u) for distinct values stored before termination, with O(n) as the upper bound. The supplied array and scalar/null result are excluded.

q1Alternatives.seen-set-in-input-order: Correct and the fixed target; the first hit is exactly the earliest second occurrence.
q1Alternatives.occurrence-count-map-in-order: Correct for every input, but it first reads the entire event array to build frequencies and then needs a second pass. That work and map are removable: the seen-set scan can return as soon as the first repeated event determines the answer. Both approaches have the same expected asymptotic time and space classes; partial reflects the explicit early-stop objective, not a different Big-O class.
q1Alternatives.compare-all-earlier-pairs: Correct but brute force, with O(n²) comparisons in the worst case and O(1) extra space.
q1Alternatives.sort-before-finding-duplicate: Incorrect because sorting discards the order of second occurrences; [20, 3, 20, 3] is a counterexample.

q2Options.linear-expected-set-space: Correct under the explicit expected/amortized hash-operation model.
q2Options.linear-constant-space: Incorrect: the set may contain every distinct identifier before termination.
q2Options.quadratic-constant-space: Incorrect for the fixed method; the set avoids repeated pairwise comparisons.
q2Options.n-log-n-linear-space: Incorrect for the fixed method; it scans with a set and does not sort.

methodReveal.title: Check prior membership in event order
methodReveal.description: Visit each identifier from left to right. If it is already in the set, return it immediately. Otherwise add it to the set and continue. If every event is processed without a membership hit, return null.
